title: Applied Materials Pledges $5 Billion as Modi Opens SEMICON India 2026
excerpt: Modi declared India has entered the second phase of its chip journey — 12 projects approved, a $13.5 billion mission budget — and urged semiconductor researchers abroad to join the buildout.
body:
• Applied Materials announced a $5 billion investment in India over the next decade at SEMICON India 2026, the event's biggest headline commitment.
  • PM Modi said India has entered the second phase of its semiconductor journey, with 12 chip-making projects approved and the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 budget expanded to $13.5 billion.
  • Three chip-packaging plants, including Micron's, have begun commercial production; India's chip consumption is projected to hit $110 billion by 2030.
  • Modi called on youth — "whether conducting research in India or abroad" — to join India's semiconductor buildout, with 70,000 of 1 lakh targeted engineers already trained.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday declared that India has entered the "second phase" of its semiconductor journey, opening SEMICON India 2026 with a pitch to global chipmakers — a pitch that paid off within hours when US equipment giant Applied Materials announced a $5 billion investment in India over the next decade.

Speaking at the inauguration of the three-day conclave in New Delhi, Modi said the semiconductor ecosystem is "expanding, opening new opportunities for innovation, investment and growth," and assured equipment makers: "whatever is needed for you (manufacturers) to succeed, government is taking all steps and efforts."

The $5 billion headline

Applied Materials, one of the world's largest semiconductor equipment makers, said its India investment would center on research, supply chain scale-up and workforce growth. The announcement came as more than 600 companies and representatives from 52 countries gathered for India's flagship chip conference.

https://x.com/ANI/status/2100465991964889588

The timing is charged. Washington and Beijing have imposed tit-for-tat export restrictions on chip technology, and the industry is in a global scramble for chip production capacity sharpened by surging AI computing demand. India, Modi said, is preparing itself as a "trusted" manufacturing location: "The world stands in utmost need of new and reliable manufacturing locations."

Where India stands

The numbers Modi put on the table: 12 chip-making projects approved under India's incentive program over the past five years; three chip-packaging plants — including one run by US memory maker Micron — now in commercial production; and the India Semiconductor Mission 2.0 budget expanded to $13.5 billion, up from $8 billion in the first phase. The government has committed more than $21 billion across its two semiconductor incentive programs.

Government estimates put India's semiconductor consumption at $45-50 billion this year, projected to reach as much as $110 billion by 2030. A recent PIB release noted India already hosts about 7% of the world's semiconductor Global Capability Centres and employs nearly 20% of the global chip design workforce.

The talent play

Modi's sharpest appeal was to people, not companies. The government has set a target of training 1 lakh engineering students for the semiconductor industry, with over 70,000 already trained under programs including the Chips-to-Startup initiative across 113 institutions.

"I call upon the youth — whether they are conducting research in India or abroad — to come forward and participate in the development of advanced technology here."

— Prime Minister Narendra Modi, SEMICON India 2026

Diaspora Angle

The diaspora talent angle is the story's engine: Indians design a fifth of the world's chips but build almost none, and Modi is explicitly recruiting semiconductor researchers working abroad — in Silicon Valley and beyond — to come back and build fabs and design houses at home.

What's Next

Modi stressed the effort goes beyond "one fab or one chip manufacturing plant" — with compound semiconductors, silicon photonics and ATMP/OSAT expansion all under Semicon 2.0's six pillars. The question now is execution: whether India's approved projects move from packaging and pilots to full fabrication at global scale.
